opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we think about a lot, because the whole premise of a world foundation model is that it shouldn't be tied to one particular robot. If you train only on data from a single arm in a single lab, the model learns that embodiment very well, but it doesn't learn the physics of the world. So our starting point is to separate two things: what is universal about the physical world, and what is specific to a given body.

The universal part is things like gravity, contact, friction, how objects deform, how liquids pour, how light interacts with surfaces, and cause and effect over time. You can learn a lot of that from very diverse video. That includes human activity, driving, industrial settings, kitchens, and warehouses. Humans are, in a sense, the most widely deployed "robot" in the world, so first-person and third-person video of people manipulating objects is enormously valuable. It shows intent, it shows hands interacting with things, and it covers a long tail of situations that no robot fleet has seen yet.

Then there's embodiment data, meaning actual robot trajectories with actions, proprioception, and camera views from different platforms: arms, grippers, dexterous hands, humanoids, mobile bases, autonomous vehicles. The key choice here is breadth over depth. We would rather have many different embodiments with moderate amounts of data each than a huge amount from one. When the model sees the same kind of task done by very different bodies, it's forced to learn the task-level and physics-level structure rather than memorizing one kinematic chain.

Curation matters more than raw volume. Most raw video on the internet is not useful for physical AI. It's static, it's edited with cuts, it has text overlays, or nothing physically interesting happens. So we invest heavily in filtering for things like motion, interaction, camera stability, and physical plausibility. We also annotate with rich descriptions so the model can connect language to what's happening physically. A smaller, well-curated set can beat a much larger noisy one.

Simulation and synthetic data are another lever, especially for coverage. With simulation you can vary lighting, materials, object geometry, and robot morphology in a controlled way, and you get ground truth for free. But we're careful about the sim-to-real gap, so we treat synthetic data as a complement for diversity and edge cases, not a replacement for real-world footage.

Finally, we evaluate transfer directly. We don't just look at whether generated video looks pretty. We ask whether the model's predictions are physically consistent, and whether a policy or a post-trained model on a new robot benefits from the pretraining. If adding a data source doesn't improve downstream behavior on embodiments the model hasn't seen, that tells us something about whether that data is really teaching general physics or just adding noise.

So in short: diverse real-world video for physical common sense, a broad mix of embodiments for action grounding, strong curation, simulation for coverage, and evaluation focused on transfer rather than appearance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The first thing I'd say is that we try not to think about data as "data for this robot" or "data for that robot." If you select training data around a specific embodiment, you've already lost the transfer game, because what you learn is tangled up with that particular arm, that particular gripper, that particular camera placement. So the question we ask instead is: what does a model need to see in order to understand how the physical world behaves, independent of who is acting in it?

That reframing leads to a layered approach. The base of it is a very large amount of general video of the world — people doing things, objects falling, liquids pouring, things being pushed, occluded, deformed. Humans are, in a sense, the most diverse embodiment there is, and human video is abundant. From that, the model learns physics, object permanence, contact, cause and effect. None of that cares whether the actuator is a seven-degree-of-freedom arm or a humanoid hand.

On top of that we add robot data, but we're deliberate about covering many embodiments rather than going deep on one. The point is not to teach the model to control any specific robot. It's to teach it the mapping between an action and its consequence across very different bodies, so that when a new robot shows up, it's an interpolation problem rather than something totally out of distribution. We also put a lot of care into how actions and observations are represented, because if every robot has its own idiosyncratic action space, the model can't share anything across them.

The third ingredient is synthetic and generated data. Real robot data is expensive and, frankly, boring — it's biased toward whatever was easy to collect in a few labs. Simulation and generation let us fill in the long tail: unusual lighting, cluttered scenes, failure cases, rare interactions. And importantly, we can render the same scenario from many embodiments and many viewpoints, which is almost a direct way of forcing the representation to be embodiment-agnostic.

Finally, we're quite aggressive about curation. Scale alone doesn't give you transfer; you need diversity along the axes that matter — objects, scenes, dynamics, viewpoints — and you need to filter out data that looks different on the surface but is actually redundant. We measure this empirically: we hold out entire robots and entire environments, and we ask whether the model generalizes to them. If adding a slice of data doesn't improve held-out transfer, it doesn't earn its place, no matter how large it is.

So in short: learn the world first, learn embodiment second, and keep testing whether what you learned actually moves across bodies.

astra-6.text:
I would start with the physical capabilities we want to transfer, rather than with a particular robot. Things like understanding how objects move, how contact changes a scene, and what happens when an action succeeds or fails. Then I’d choose data that shows those interactions across different environments, viewpoints, objects, and robot configurations.

The important distinction is between shared physical knowledge and the specifics of an embodiment. Two robots might have different joints or grippers, but both need to understand that an object can slip or that pushing it off-center can make it rotate. You want the data to support that shared understanding while preserving enough information about each robot’s actions and constraints.

And I’d judge the selection by transfer: hold out a robot or an environment and test whether the learned knowledge actually helps. More data is useful, but coverage of meaningful physical interactions—and evidence that it generalizes—is what I’d prioritize.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start with the capabilities we want to transfer, rather than with a particular robot. Can the model understand how objects move, what happens when they make contact, and how an action changes the scene? Those are useful across different embodiments.

Then I would choose data with diversity in environments, objects, viewpoints, and interactions. For robotics data, we also need to know the embodiment—its sensors, geometry, and action space—so the model can distinguish general physical behavior from the way a particular robot executes a task.

The key test is to hold out a robot or an environment during training and evaluate transfer there. If performance improves only on robots already represented in the data, we haven't demonstrated the generalization we're looking for. That evaluation should guide which data we collect next.
